meta.title: The Eisman Playbook Decoded
meta.subtitle: Every episode of Steve Eisman's podcast, read end to end, including the paid tier. The recurring theses, the guest bench, the frameworks he teaches, and the calls he made, tracked as they changed. Third edition, current to 25 September 2026: 152 episodes with a synopsis each, 92 interviews and lectures with a full dossier, and every premium subscriber episode read.

blocks.v: The podcast launched on 5 June 2025 and has run without a real break since. A strict weekly rhythm holds it together, and the two halves of that rhythm do entirely different jobs.

v.label: Mondays
v.p: Forty-five to eighty minutes. One expert, usually a sell-side or boutique analyst rather than a famous name, taken through a single sector in forensic depth. Eisman plays the intelligent generalist and interrupts constantly to make the guest define terms. Since roughly Episode 50 he closes each one with a solo lessons-learned coda.

v.label: Fridays
v.p: Twenty to thirty-five minutes, solo and scripted. Index statistics, then earnings walked company by company, then a mailbag answering listener questions. It began as The Friday Market Wrap and became The Weekly Wrap around September 2025. Here his own views run undiluted, across 57 episodes.

blocks.v: Three other formats sit on top. Masterclass lectures on the 2008 crisis, financial literacy and private credit run as university lectures with no guest. Panels gather three analysts at once. Reaction episodes include one where he watches scenes from The Big Short and marks what the film got right.

He frames the show as apolitical and says so repeatedly. This is a business and markets podcast, he takes government policy as given, and he will not tell anyone how to vote. A disclaimer closes every episode.
In the business world, we don't call the game. We just take the pitches.
His authority on the show rests on a specific career shape, and he returns to it constantly, because he learned nearly every framework he teaches at one of these stops.

rows: Penn, then Harvard Law
Practised law briefly and did securitisation document work for The Money Store, which is how he later got the subprime beat.
Oppenheimer, sell-side analyst

A banker walked into his office and handed him subprime coverage almost by accident. He built out to subprime mortgage, subprime auto, Fannie, Freddie, Sallie Mae, credit cards, asset managers and investment banks, and taught himself to model.
Buy side, large hedge fund
Picked up banks and the whole insurance sector for the first time.
FrontPoint Partners, portfolio manager
The Big Short years. He ran a long-short financials equity book and a credit default swap book against subprime paper at the same time.
Emrys Partners, founder
His own fund, later wound down.
Neuberger Berman, managing director
Ran the Eisman Group inside private asset management.
2025 onward
The Real Eisman Playbook
Podcast, Substack and YouTube channel, managing his own money.

blocks.v: Steve Carell played him in the 2015 film of Michael Lewis's The Big Short, a fact he treats with visible ambivalence. He corrects the film's details often and dismisses the perpetual-crisis punditry the fame invites. He left Neuberger Berman after the firm placed him on indefinite leave in September 2024 over a social media post about Gaza that it called irresponsible and objectionable. He deleted his X account at the time. The podcast is his post-institutional act.

Two other pieces of context surface on the show itself. He disclosed his breast cancer diagnosis on air on 19 July 2025, in that week's wrap, and framed it deliberately: he wanted men to know the disease is not confined to women. A February 2026 episode looked back on it. He also mentions owning a small business, reads heavily in historical fiction, recommends Colleen McCullough's Rome novels, and reads comics.

sections.title: The framework he built on air

blocks.v: Unusually for a podcast, Eisman formalises his own thinking twice a year and then holds himself to it. Two documents matter more than any single episode.
The four themes of 2025 (19 December 2025)

v: The K-shaped economy. GDP growth is real but concentrated almost entirely in AI capital spending.
The AI revolution, or an AI bubble. He refuses to pick, deliberately.
Fears about the growth in private credit. Note the word fears. At that point he would not call it a problem.
Affordability. The cumulative effect of inflation on the consumer, not the current rate.

blocks.v: The five structural themes for 2026 (9 January 2026)
These are longer-arc claims about market structure rather than year-ahead calls. The through-line: the S&P has become something other than a mirror of the American economy.

v: Tech and tech-related stocks dominate the index to a degree no other developed market approaches, above 40%, and by his mid-2026 count closer to 50%.
Consumers drive roughly 70% of the US economy, yet consumer stocks drive less and less of the index.
Index investing reinforces the concentration. About 60% of flows go into funds that mechanically buy what they already own, in the size they already own it.
The market has therefore come unmoored from everyday life. Whole sectors can rot without the index noticing.
Any real break will therefore be violent. Passive flows that push a market up smoothly reverse without a bid.

blocks.v: Even if parts of the K-shaped economy get worse, even if the overall economy stagnates, the market might, I repeat, might power through it. As long as current tech and AI trends remain intact. However, if AI trends falter, I would expect an enormous correction.
That sentence carries more weight than anything else on the show. Nearly every other position follows from it.

Read in order, the 152 episodes tell a single story: a market that began the period celebrating AI capital spending and ended it auditing every dollar of it. Along the way the show absorbed a war, a government shutdown, a private credit panic and the host's cancer treatment, without missing a week.

v.p: The establishing phase. Launch with Patrick McGee on Apple, the short-selling pair with Ganapathi and Safalow, the Melissa Lee role reversal, and the first statements of method. AI is the market's engine and capex announcements are unambiguous buy signals.

The vocabulary arrives. He names the K-shaped economy, splits 89 reporting companies into AI and everything else, and starts asking the return-on-invested-capital question out loud. Sorkin's 1929 book gives the season its historical frame: credit plus leverage plus FOMO.

The two-sided market. Nvidia accelerates at a 4.4 trillion market cap and the tape sells off anyway. Burry's depreciation argument, the Ferguson railroad analogy and the binding constraint framework (power) all enter the show's standing repertoire. The year ends with the four themes codified and the 2008 masterclasses delivered.

The repricing begins. Gary Marcus makes the scaling-sceptic case; Daniel Guetta answers that good enough already disrupts. Software becomes guilty until proven innocent, the SaaSpocalypse gets its name, and identical capex headlines start sinking the stocks they once lifted. He finishes chemotherapy and thanks Valerie Feigen on air.

The stress tests. The Iran war suspends stock-level analysis for weeks, oil breaches 100 dollars, and private credit cracks in public: Blue Owl gates redemptions, Gober lays out the life insurance triangle, and Eisman's sharpest line lands, executives mistaking a benign cycle for genius.

The single trade. Premium launches with A Conspiracy of Credit. The 10-year breaches his 4.5% Rubicon and he lightens up. Hyperscalers turn to shareholders to fund capex, Google raises 85 billion, and he concludes the stock and bond markets have collapsed into one AI bet.

The audit. Torsten Slok puts AI at roughly half of US growth. Free cash flow at the hyperscalers goes negative, a credit cycle forms inside the AI trade, and he names the single point of failure: the day Anthropic and OpenAI stop buying compute. The Strategas pair close the corpus by raising the rate threshold the market just absorbed.

The bill arrives in rates. The war heats up again, oil nears 110 dollars, the Fed raises by 25 basis points to 3.75 to 4%, and the ten-year runs through 4.9% to a multi-year high above 5.1%. He concedes his 4.5% line was wrong, moves it to 5%, and says a correction is probably imminent if the yield holds there. He names OpenAI as the single failure that could tip the economy into recession, partially hedges his biggest gains, and lists the defensive funds he would rotate into.

blocks.v: The through line is his own subprime education applied in real time. Theses develop in stages, the data decides, and the job is to know the argument well enough to measure its risk before the market forces the question.

He starts using the phrase around October 2025 and it becomes the show's organising metaphor, appearing in 27 episodes. The claim is arithmetic before it is rhetorical. US GDP grew roughly 2% in 2025, which on a base near 25 trillion dollars comes to about 500 billion, and AI-related capital spending for the year ran north of 400 billion. Strip that out and growth rounds to nothing.

items: Hyperscalers, semiconductors, Nvidia and its supply chain
Power and grid: GE Vernova, Vertiv, turbines, small modular reactors
Industrials, but only where AI-adjacent
Investment banking, M&A advisory, trading
The top 10% of households, who account for nearly half of all consumer spending
Housing and the whole housing ecosystem
Consumer staples, with Procter organic growth at zero and McCormick weak
Domino's, which he calls the poster child
Residential solar, obliterated
Subprime auto, with 60-day delinquencies at 6.65%, the highest since 1994
Youth employment, and computer science graduates in particular

blocks.v: He checks the claim against the market with one tell he repeats: the gap between the S&P 500 and the S&P 500 equal-weight index. In 2025 the cap-weighted index rose about 16% while equal-weight managed 10%, and 37% of index constituents finished the year down.

He is careful about what this does not mean. On its own it produces no recession. His stated recession tripwire is bank credit quality, and through mid-2026 he reads it as benign. On Episode 68, Torsten Slok adds the decomposition Eisman then adopts: the K exists in three separate dimensions, wealth, wage growth and inflation exposure, with the bottom cohort spending a larger share on food, energy and housing.

He also rejects the fatalistic reading. When a viewer commented that a K-shaped economy has always existed, he disagreed. The distribution may be unfair, but everyone is materially wealthier than before, and he cites John Cassidy, a critic of capitalism, conceding the same point.

sections.title: AI: he will not call it

blocks.v: This is the most-covered subject on the show and the one where his position visibly moves. He owns the stocks, says so constantly, and narrates his own growing discomfort instead of resolving it. Tracked chronologically, the arc is the most valuable thing in the corpus.

v.p: Nvidia posts 69% year-over-year revenue growth. He calls the AI story still in its infancy and says the US economy is more dynamic than at any point in his lifetime. Only a trade war could derail it.

Morgan Stanley's 2.9 trillion dollar data-centre estimate through 2028 lands. He notes approvingly that roughly half comes from hyperscaler operating cash flow, which he calls healthy and the key distinction from the dot-com bubble.
The K-shape framing arrives. He admits for the first time to a twitch in the back of his eyeball after a long bullish run.

Michael Burry argues hyperscalers stretched compute depreciation from three to five years out to five or six, inflating earnings. Eisman takes it seriously but rules it academic: no catalyst forces the write-down, and auditors will not force it.

He sharpens the real risk. Not valuation, not accounting, but whether ever-larger models stop paying off. If scaling stalls, chip orders stop and the virtuous cycle reverses. He cites the estimate that big tech needs two trillion dollars of AI revenue by 2030 to justify the spend.
The Rubin chip strengthens Burry's case. Blackwell shipped in late 2024 and already looks obsolete, which sits badly against a six-year depreciation life.

The narrative inverts. Google guides to 180 billion dollars of 2026 capex, double 2025 and 60 billion above consensus, and the stock falls. Amazon guides 200 billion against 146 billion expected and drops 7%. Capex used to be a buy signal. Now it is a sell signal.

The moment he flags as a sea change. Google raises 85 billion dollars in equity rather than debt. Hyperscalers can no longer self-fund. Owning AI stocks while the AI companies foot the bill is one thing; owning them while they ask public shareholders to foot it is another.

Hyperscaler capex approaches one trillion dollars for the year. He concludes the entire market is now a single bet and identifies the Achilles heel: OpenAI and Anthropic account for roughly 70% of AI revenue at the big clouds, with cheap Chinese open-weight models threatening a price war. He reduces exposure and sells Alphabet after years of holding it.

The dependency argument narrows to one company. He calls OpenAI the Achilles heel of the US economy, citing a June quarter in which revenue rose about 1 billion dollars to 6.7 billion while costs rose about 3 billion to 12.3 billion, and argues its failure would cause an almost immediate recession because AI spending is carrying GDP growth. He dismisses the AI extinction talk from Anthropic and OpenAI as convenient, since neither can afford a slowdown, and adds an accounting charge: data centers financed off balance sheet through vehicles like Meta's Beignet, 80% owned by Blue Owl and Pimco, echo Enron and the 2008 SIVs. His own position follows: he is more and more nervous, will not add AI risk even indirectly through investment banks, and has partially hedged his largest gains.

blocks.v: The four arguments he keeps separate
He refuses to call it partly because people keep collapsing four distinct questions into one.

rows: Will language models scale to general intelligence?
Outside his expertise, so he leans on Gary Marcus, who says no. He treats this as the fundamental risk to the whole story.
Is there a capex bubble?
A different question entirely. Real orders from real companies, unlike 1999. But outside capital increasingly funds it.
Are the accounts honest?
Burry is probably right on depreciation, but nothing forces the issue, so it does not trade.
Are there moats?
His growing worry. If the models are near-identical and commoditising, the spend has no defensible return.

blocks.v: The trigger he watches is a single hyperscaler cutting capital spending. He says repeatedly that the day Meta announces a 25% cut, the market goes straight down, and that by the time it shows up in a print it is already too late. Stacy Rasgon, the semiconductor analyst on Episode 63, agrees on the mechanism and disagrees on the timing, arguing capex is if anything too low.
The SaaSpocalypse

Software is the corollary trade, and he treats it as structurally impaired rather than cheap. AI threatens seat-based pricing and terminal value at once, valuations have halved, and the group trades at a discount to the S&P for arguably the first time in its history. He reads that as a symptom, not a signal, because software investors have never cared about valuation. Buying it, he says on Episode 54, is catching a falling knife.
He draws one exception: proprietary data beats AI disruption. Moody's held up where S&P Global wobbled, because when a company owns a proprietary database, AI inroads become difficult to impossible.

This is the most intellectually honest sequence on the show. He begins as the sceptic of the sceptics and ends as the house bear, and the reason he gives for changing is that the data finally arrived.

The starting position, June 2025. People are calling private credit a bubble. He will not, because no credit-quality data exists. He contrasts this with 2006, when he and his team subscribed to the Moody's securitisation database and watched delinquencies deteriorate month by month like a Rosetta Stone. His refrain through most of 2025: it will not cause a recession, but when a recession comes, whoever made mistakes gets exposed.

v.p: Tricolor and First Brands fail. He is careful to note both were bank loans rather than private credit, yet the market shoots the private credit stocks anyway. He flags this as a lesson in narrative rather than fundamentals.

Blue Owl rescinds a fund merger after investors complain. He starts dissecting the BDC fee structure: fees charged on gross assets at up to two-to-one leverage, which mechanically rewards maximum leverage, with managers in the upside and out of the downside.
Blue Owl restricts redemptions. He calls retail distribution of illiquid long-dated loans with quarterly liquidity a ticking time bomb, and predicts more gates.

The prediction lands. Apollo's 25 billion dollar flagship receives an 11.2% redemption notice and honours only the 5% cap. Blackstone's BCred takes 7.9% against a 5% cap and self-funds rather than gate. Moody's downgrades a KKR-linked fund to junk. The sector is down 24% to 31% for the year.
The verdict sentence: an entire generation of private credit executives has mistaken the absence of a credit cycle for genius.
Episode 72, Private Credit's Clock is Ticking.

blocks.v: The three structural objections

v.p: Eighty percent of US direct lending goes to companies backed by private equity. The largest private credit fund, BCred, is a non-traded BDC wholly owned by Blackstone. One arm of the firm buys companies and another lends the money to buy them. As he puts it, if that sounds circular, it is only because it is.

Private credit is over-indexed to software buyouts, publicly estimated at 20% to 25% of the market and, per a Wall Street Journal piece he cites, understated. Slok puts it near 500 billion dollars of a two trillion dollar direct-lending market. Here is the collision: the sector most exposed to AI disruption is the sector private credit lent into most heavily, at high valuations, with rates higher for longer.

The one he calls potentially systemic, explored across several episodes with the former insurance examiner Tom Gober. Private equity firms own life insurers and sell their own originated paper into those captives, then use offshore captive reinsurance in Vermont, Bermuda or Barbados to lever further than onshore statements reveal. Two things changed over twenty years: riskier assets, and hidden leverage. He discloses no position, long or short.

blocks.v: Where he stops short. He does not think this is 2008 again, and says so plainly. The banks are genuinely well capitalised this time. Expect losses and possibly a recession, not systemic collapse. His reason for focusing here at all is a pattern rule rather than alarm: when a credit cycle turns, problems surface where the growth was, and private credit grew from roughly 300 billion dollars a decade ago to somewhere between 1.8 and 3 trillion.

sections.title: Affordability, and why housing is broken

blocks.v: This is his most policy-forward argument, and the one where he insists most firmly that the consensus diagnosis is wrong.
This is not a demand problem. If we could build affordable homes, people would buy them in a heartbeat.
blocks.cite: Repeated across wraps, December 2025 to March 2026

blocks.v: A politician's instinct, he argues, always reaches for a demand-side fix: subsidies, credits, rate relief. He says the binding constraint is supply, and specifically local. Zoning and permitting rules run slow, add materially to cost, and in many places make smaller homes illegal to build. His test for political seriousness is explicit. A president who tackles the local rules means it; anything else is theatre.

On the stocks, homebuilders remain rate-sensitive and no one escapes that. Through the period they have propped up volume with incentives and rate buy-downs financed through captive mortgage arms, which protects volume and destroys margin. He has been clear this can only run so far, then bought Meritage Homes in January 2026 anyway, on the rule of thumb that you buy builders at or below tangible book. He later interviewed its chief executive on air while disclosing the position.

He separates today's housing problem from 2008 emphatically. Capital requirements after Dodd-Frank made subprime mortgages uneconomic for banks. In 2006 originations of 600 billion dollars made up 20% of the mortgage market, and that industry effectively no longer exists. Today's problem is affordability and supply, not credit.
Banks are safe, and he is the one saying it

Coming from the man who shorted them into the crisis, this is his most counterintuitive standing position. He credits a specific mechanism. Dodd-Frank created the Fed's vice chair for financial supervision, and he notes how astonishing it is that the United States had no head bank regulator before that. Daniel Tarullo held the role de facto, and Eisman calls him possibly the only great bank regulator in American history. Through the annual stress tests, leverage fell by more than half, and the risk tails were cut off inside that. Citigroup went from roughly 35 to 1 down to 10 to 1, a distance he likens to Pluto and the sun.

He teaches the plumbing rather than asserting the conclusion. Capital ratios divide common equity by risk-weighted assets, not by assets. The binding constraint on large banks is the stress capital buffer, not the statutory minimum. And the risk-weighted asset concept itself was, in his view, a root cause of 2008, because of the leverage it permitted. He also warns against ratcheting the test forever. Push it far enough and banking stops being an economic business.

His recession indicator is bank credit quality. As the banks go, so goes the economy was his line for a year, until July 2026, when he revised it. This time the banks are not the leading indicator, because the economy's fate now hinges on AI. He also argues repeatedly for a wave of regional bank consolidation.

The merger wave he wanted is not coming, and he says so. His two-part paid lecture on analysing banks in September 2026 restates the case for regional consolidation, since technology costs favour scale and JPMorgan's deposit share has roughly doubled since the crisis, then abandons it as an investment case. Bank chief executives like being bank chief executives, and First Horizon, the obvious target, declared itself a buyer. His advice now is to stick to the large banks and to buy even those only after recession fears have crushed their valuations.
The Fed and the dollar

He dismisses two popular anxieties. On the dollar losing reserve status, people have worried for forty years without asking why it never happens. His answer: the global system runs on Treasuries, through the repo market and sovereign wealth allocation, and no alternative exists. Not crypto, which is too small. Not Chinese bonds. Not European ones. Given an alternative he would worry about deficits; absent one, he does not. On the deficit generally, he calls the public hand-wringing Wall Street's version of virtue signalling.
On Greenspan he is unsparing. History will not be kind, because Greenspan allowed the leverage, and people told him directly about fraud in the subprime market in 2005 and 2006, and he did not care.

The Fed turned in September 2026. With the war pushing oil toward 110 dollars and inflation fears back, the Fed raised by 25 basis points to a range of 3.75 to 4% and pencilled in another increase, in defiance of the White House. It is the first rate increase in the sixteen months the corpus covers, and it arrives with the ten-year above 5%.

His crypto critique is narrow, and he repeats it almost verbatim across dozens of episodes. He does not argue it is worthless. He admits owning a little, just so he is there. He argues the price action falsifies the stated thesis.
Bitcoin acts contrary to its own thesis.

Holders justify it as a hedge against fiat debasement. Were that true it would rise on days of fear. It falls on those days, correlating with tech stocks. Whatever it is, it is not the thing its owners say it is. He adds a separate worry: the risk sits less in the asset class than in the players and the infrastructure, and he names venues like Binance as the source of the violent volatility.

Stablecoins he treats as a genuinely interesting payments question, and explains carefully. Not a cryptocurrency, but the same underlying technology. You hand over dollars, the issuer buys Treasuries, and crucially you need a network to move the money. That last point drives his conclusion. Circle and Tether are challenging Visa and Mastercard, who already own trusted global networks. He doubts disintermediation in payments and thinks remittances is the beachhead that actually works, a far easier market to break than the card rails.

This generalises into one of his firmest sector views. Payments is a brutal, hyper-competitive space where nearly everyone attacks everyone else's business, and only Visa and Mastercard hold genuinely impregnable franchises. He owns Visa. He watched Fiserv collapse and PayPal struggle and treats both as confirmation.
Scattered across the wraps and the financial literacy masterclass sits a fairly complete statement of how he works.
Core operating rules

v: He is not a trader. He does not trade in and out of quarters. He studies macro and micro trends, builds an investment story with long-term potential, and takes a full position on conviction.

Buy market power. His most consistent screen: proprietary products, duopolies, pricing power. Moody's, Visa, T-Mobile, Progressive. Without a proprietary product, as with Super Micro and Dell, you get price wars and margin compression.

Know your thesis and its falsifiers. Always know what would disprove you. He names the failure mode thesis creep, quietly rewriting the thesis as the stock moves and letting the tail wag the dog, and says flatly that every investor eventually succumbs.
Balance sheets matter as much as income statements, and sometimes more. His teaching case is the MLP collapse, where investors who read only the income statement got wiped out.
In good times people care about stories. In bad times they care about balance sheets.
All my best ideas are stolen. He rates boutique research above bulge-bracket, subscribes widely, and treats talking to people as equal in value to staring at screens.
Pay for the data nobody else buys. The Moody's securitisation database is the origin of this rule, and the absence of any equivalent is exactly why he distrusts private credit.

Measure risk with beta, not stress tests. He tried the expensive scenario services and found them useless. They told him he would lose money in a crash, which he knew. Position-level and portfolio-level beta is the pragmatic tool.

Watch correlation between longs and shorts. Long Goldman and short FICO is a real hedge, because the theses are independent. Long every automaker and short every carriage maker is one bet wearing two hats.
Charts are a tool, not a substitute. After a collapse he waits for a base before buying. If a chart on something he owns deteriorates, he rechecks the fundamentals.
Do not invest overseas. A stated personal preference, on the grounds that the United States is the most dynamic developed economy.
Turnarounds are fixer-uppers or gut renovations. Know which one you bought. UnitedHealth investors thought they had the former.

blocks.v: What he says about chief executives

A recurring panel subject. The good ones share a willingness to go against the grain and absorb severe criticism for it, and Jamie Dimon is the consensus best in financial services. The bad ones share balance sheets that grew too fast, absent controls and high-risk lending. His nuance on Dimon: being a great chief executive does not make you right when you pontificate about policy, and Dimon was wrong about Tarullo forcing banks to delever too far.

His case study in a chief executive who was good, mediocre and bad in sequence is Hank Greenberg, whom he shorted at AIG in 2005 as his largest position. Greenberg built a powerhouse, ran it so loosely that AIG Financial Products could write credit default swaps on tens of billions of subprime unsupervised, and left behind a company with 200 operating systems that took fifteen years to fix. His summary: a chief executive who stays too long becomes all three.
On mergers: doing the deal is half of the first inning. Integration is eight or nine tenths of the game.

sections.title: Staged disagreement: how he actually uses guests

blocks.v: The guest list looks like a parade of sell-side analysts. Watched closely, it is something more deliberate: he books his own opposition, stages second opinions against his own guests, and runs multi-episode investigations that individual episodes only hint at.

v.p: Gary Marcus makes the LLM-sceptic case in January; Daniel Guetta, a Columbia professor who built the systems, answers in February; Marcus returns in June. Eisman sides with neither and keeps the only question that matters, returns on the spend, explicitly open.

Tom Gober's forensic alarm on private equity in life insurance is followed within weeks by Tom Gallagher of Evercore, who is broadly comfortable. Eisman admits on air he expected the veteran to be more scared. He aired both anyway.

Healthcare runs as a four-part inquiry across five months: Michael Ha on the UnitedHealth collapse, Warris Bokhari on claim denials, Mark Cuban on drug pricing, then Ha again on whether any insurer is investable. Each episode inherits the last one's open questions.

blocks.v: The bench also widened in kind. The first management interview arrives in November 2025 (Glass House Brands, with his shareholding disclosed up front), followed by the Meritage Homes chief executive inside a wrap, Amy Butte on taking companies public, and Apollo's head of originations answering the private credit critique from inside the machine. Operators joined the analysts once the show had standing questions only operators could answer.

Two guests interview him: Melissa Lee of CNBC in the August 2025 role reversal, and Ivy Zelman hosting the Case Western event where he retells 2008 for students. And one pattern holds across all 69 people indexed in this corpus: when a guest disagrees with the host, the disagreement survives the edit.

Version two noted that he books his own opposition. The dossiers show it is a repeatable procedure with a fixed shape: air the alarming case, name the discomfort, book the credible opposite, then state which way he moved and what stays open.

rows: Gary Marcus, 19 January 2026, scaling is a dead end and hallucination is architectural
Daniel Guetta, 16 February 2026, a practitioner who agrees on AGI and says it does not matter
Sided slightly with Guetta on usefulness, refused both men on returns, then rebooked Marcus in June
Tom Gober, 2 March 2026, private equity has turned life insurers into captive buyers
Tom Gallagher, 15 June 2026, a decades-trusted analyst who is broadly comfortable
Kept the thesis, narrowed the target to smaller insurers, kept the sector as a monitoring post
His own private credit bearishness, running since late 2025
Chris Edson of Apollo, 27 April 2026, answering from inside the machine
Conceded Apollo's software exposure is genuinely small, kept the view that a credit cycle is coming through software
Michael Ha, 22 September 2025, UnitedHealth is structurally impaired
Michael Ha again, 23 March 2026, after six months of evidence
No counterweight booked, because the first call kept being right. He ends more bearish instead

blocks.v: The procedure has one honest limit, and the dossiers make it visible. When he agrees with a guest at the outset, no counterweight gets booked at all. The Glass House management interview, the cannabis position he had already taken, and the Meritage interview, a stock he had already recommended, are both conducted as friendly examinations. He discloses the holding in each case, which is the safeguard he actually applies, but nobody is invited to argue the other side.
What the disagreements have in common

v: Disagreement survives the edit. George Noble's gold thesis, Itay Michaeli's Tesla constructiveness, Adrian Wooldridge relaying Greenspan's account of the crisis: in each case the guest's position is left standing and Eisman's objection is stated beside it rather than over it.
He scores himself out loud. The Noble episode ends with an explicit tally: open-minded but unconvinced on energy rotation, a declared skeptic on gold, in complete agreement on crypto.

Panels are used for coverage, not for conflict. The three Evercore analysts on the consumer, the two MoffettNathanson analysts on media, and the Strategas pair are booked to cover a surface, and he synthesizes rather than adjudicates.

The strongest pushback is procedural. His most effective move is not a counter-thesis, it is a disclosure question the guest cannot answer, which is how the UnitedHealth gain-on-sale detail and the FICO pricing history both surface.

sections.title: His disclosed portfolio, from the source

blocks.v: Versions one and two reconstructed this from positions mentioned across the public episodes, and got it materially wrong. The paid episode of 1 July 2026 states the book in full, and it is shorter and more concentrated than the public mentions implied. He holds 16 longs, groups them into five themes of his own naming, and explains each one. What follows replaces the earlier reconstruction.

His stated method sits alongside it: he has run 15 to 30 longs for years and is at the low end now after pruning, he almost never trades, he takes a full position rather than leveraging in slowly, and he sells when the thesis breaks rather than when the price moves. The discipline he names as hardest is guarding against thesis creep, finding a fresh reason to keep owning something after the original reason died.

items: Nvidia. The bellwether. First-quarter revenue growth of 85%, and a one-year-out multiple near 23 times, which he calls not expensive for that growth. Needs no capital
Arista. Bought once he realised data centers need more than chips. Roughly 45 times 2026, so no room for error: it fell 14% on a first quarter that beat but did not raise enough
Microsoft. Cut back, on the software disruption debate and the possibility it must raise capital. Roughly 23 times 2026
Amazon. Held for the cloud business, which he calls a necessary AI investment. Roughly 27 times 2026

GE Vernova. His best pick ever. Pitched to him near 165 after the 2024 spin, against his own scepticism from watching GE for decades; market value near 250 billion at recording. Expensive at roughly 45 times, defended on visibility
Quanta. The same thesis one step along: rising electrical demand means new plants, and Quanta builds them. Roughly 50 times 2026
Eaton. The disappointment he names as such. First-quarter earnings growth of 3%, dragged by its non-data-center businesses. He says his patience is not infinite

Charter. Roughly 3 times 2026 earnings, on capital spending falling from 11 billion in 2026 toward 7.5 to 8 billion by 2028, converting to buybacks. He owns the bad quarter: 120,000 broadband subscribers lost against a 100,000 estimate
Meritage Homes. At 1.0 times tangible book while profitable, retiring roughly 11% of shares this year, with a homebuilder takeover wave printing at 1.25 to 1.3 times book
AIG. The Citigroup analogy: a subpar 8% return on equity and 1.05 times book, now a pure property and casualty business, with Chubb and Travelers near two times book as the gap to close

v.h: Great franchises, five, plus one speculation
items: Apple. Not an AI builder, so no capital raise, but any AI company reaching consumers may have to go through it. The risk he names is China manufacturing
Moody's and Visa. The duopolies he says he loves, with the caveats that ratings track issuance and payment volume tracks the economy
Progressive. Possibly the best insurance company in the world, in a pricing trough that puts 2026 earnings growth at negative 11%
Eli Lilly. Won the GLP-1 war outright, with earnings growth of 100%, then 86%, then roughly 50% expected, against Novo Nordisk going negative

Glass House Brands. Explicitly speculative and not for everyone. Priced near 13 against his own three scenarios of 40, 49 and 58, on cannabis rescheduling opening states where the price is roughly 800 a pound against 200 in California

blocks.v: What he sold, and why it matters

The single most informative disclosure is the exit. He sold Alphabet, Meta and Oracle, three long-held AI positions, on one argument: the business model changed underneath them. Software used to be capital light, and Microsoft last raised capital when it went public in 1986. Now Alphabet's capital spending runs from 90 billion in 2025 to 180 to 190 billion, it has raised 85 billion in equity, Oracle is raising, and he expects Meta and Microsoft to follow. His conclusion is that investors will rotate away from the hyperscalers that need capital and toward the power, semiconductor and equipment names that do not, which is exactly the shape of the book above.

v.label: Short
items: Fair Isaac (FICO), on the thesis that its consumer scoring monopoly is eroding
Trupanion, disclosed in September 2026: short for years, a product he likes and a business he calls bad

v.label: Sold in 2026
items: Alphabet
Meta
Oracle
Charter, capitulated 31 July 2026, after this episode

v.label: Explicitly not held
items: Tesla, previously shorted, and he says he got his head handed to him
Any bank, the last was Citigroup, right thesis and wrong management
Any private credit name, long or short
Bonds and commodities, and he does not count his home as an investment

blocks.v: Since the disclosure

September 2026 changes the risk rather than the names. He says he has partially shorted some of his high flyers against the box in his own account, to protect large embedded gains through the autumn, and calls it a timing decision rather than a verdict on the companies; he intends to close the short near year end and take the risk back in 2027. Nvidia is his worked example, not a named trade. Listeners pointed out that the tax code treats this as a constructive sale, and he accepted the limits on air. He also names the defensive funds he would move toward if the ten-year holds above 5%, a low-volatility dividend fund, a low-volatility S&P fund and a property and casualty insurance fund, while saying he has not made that call yet. In the Big Short reunion, he and one of his former partners both say they own Glass House Brands. He was tempted to short AeroVironment on its drone pricing and did not.

He also names the four conditions that would change the book: hard evidence that data centers are much harder to build and open than assumed, evidence of companies backing away from AI on usage cost, a ten-year yield holding above 4.5% for more than a few weeks, which would send him toward defensives that are not rate sensitive, and a weakening economy, which would open short opportunities. Failing those, he says he would rather hold and not pay the capital gains.
Guarding against thesis creep is unbelievably important. No one likes to admit they have made a mistake.

One mistake he volunteers without being asked: he owned Arista and not Cisco, and says the cheaper, weaker company would have worked too, because a rising tide lifts all boats. That is the same admission pattern the errors section documents, made here about a position nobody would have known to ask about.
The show's most unusual habit is administrative: he keeps score on himself. Recommendations are dated, revisited and graded, and the failures get more airtime than the wins.

v.p: He recommends Charter Communications and Meritage Homes on air, with the theses spelled out: a free cash flow yield above 20% signals suspected bankruptcy, and the balance sheet says otherwise.
Charter falls 25% in a day. He restates the thesis publicly and adds to the position: when you recommend a stock publicly, own the bad quarter in public too.
Two bad quarters on the core metric. He opens the wrap by capitulating without hedging: bottom line, he gives up, and simply put, he made a mistake.

The threshold he held for a year gives way. Originally, he says, he thought the market could not stomach a ten-year above 4.5%, and that was wrong. He moves the line to 5% on 18 September and, a week later, with the yield at 5.1%, says a correction is probably imminent if it stays there.

blocks.v: The same register covers the older record. He shorted Tesla and got his head handed to him, which hardened the never-short-a-cult rule. He covered the Big Short trades in spring 2008 because a bailout, not the fundamentals, had become the risk, and he describes the mechanics of exiting flatly, calling swap desks and accepting their prices. Asked to name the next black swan, he answers that the question misunderstands what a black swan is.

v: Thresholds are held loosely. His 4.5% line in the sand made him lighten up in May 2026. When the market absorbed it, he said so plainly in September 2026, called it wrong, and moved the line to 5%, where it now stands as a dated test.
Timing is part of being right. A bear case a year early is indistinguishable from a wrong one, his standing warning to every would-be short seller.
Positions are opinions, not identities. On disclosing his FICO short: he is short because of the research, and he is not trying to convince anyone to join him.
Survival beats thesis quality. Being right over five years is worthless if margin forces you out in five weeks, his reading of the August 2026 hedge fund liquidation.

blocks.v: Bottom line, I give up. Simply put, I made a mistake.
blocks.cite: On Charter Communications, Weekly Wrap, 31 July 2026

sections.title: When he actually changes his mind

blocks.v: Reading the first 70 interviews and lectures for one question, what moved by the end, turns the show's stated open-mindedness into something measurable. The answer is that Eisman updates often, but along strict lines: he adopts frameworks readily, adopts timing calls almost never, and hardens fastest when a guest cannot answer a disclosure question.

v.p: When a guest supplies a way of seeing rather than a forecast, he takes it whole and redeploys it within days. Steve Tusa's proprietary versus derivative test shows up in that week's wrap. Stu Elman's venture capital depression is repeated almost verbatim to Melissa Lee the following week. Ben Kallo's physical constraint, Helima Croft's mission creep and Torsten Slok's overindexation all become standing vocabulary.

Timing is where he stops. Lakshmi Ganapathi's consumer crack gets accepted as a direction and refused as a date, twice, once with a six to nine month clock attached. Gary Marcus wins the concession that the scaling question is real and never the concession that it resolves this year. His own formulation, that a bear case a year early is indistinguishable from a wrong one, is the rule he applies to guests as well.

The interviews where nothing converges are rarely about valuation. Michael Ha twice, Kelsey Zhu on FICO and Rob Oliver on software all end with Eisman more negative than he began, and in each case the sticking point is that the numbers cannot be checked. Against a company he cannot audit, a guest's optimism moves him backwards.

blocks.v: The three admissions worth marking

v.p: He concedes his own model of 2008 was wrong in a specific way. He had assumed the authorities were knowingly slow; the archives say they were genuinely ignorant and out of bandwidth. This is the rare case of a guest correcting the episode of history Eisman is most identified with.

After booking Gary Marcus and then deliberately booking his opposite, he says on air that he sides a little more with Guetta: the products are good enough to disrupt without being intelligent. He still refuses the returns question, and dates it two years out.

He arrives primed by Tom Gober's alarm on life insurance and admits surprise that an analyst he has trusted for decades is comfortable. He does not abandon the worry, he relocates it, from the large alternative insurers to the smaller aggressive ones.

blocks.v: The solo episodes carry the two cleanest reversals, because there is no guest to credit. On 1 September 2025 he retires his own doomsayer posture, saying corrections once made him want to raise cash and no longer do. In the second 2008 masterclass he goes further and argues for a wave of bank mergers, which is the man who shorted the banks into the crisis making the case for letting them get bigger.

The 22 interviews and lectures added since fit the same shape. In September 2026 he gave up a timing call, the 4.5% threshold, the moment the market proved it wrong, and kept the framework, that some level of rates breaks the market, intact. He did the same with bank consolidation: the logic survives, the trade does not. The line he used about it is the most honest summary of the pattern in the corpus.
The only thing my thesis has going for it is its impeccable logic. But that's not enough.
blocks.cite: How to Analyze Banks, Part 2, 23 September 2026

blocks.v: Every episode synopsis in the explorer now carries a what-can-be-learned list. Read together, they resolve into a short course he never announces but teaches continuously. These are the lessons that recur most, each traceable to multiple dated episodes.

items: Watch what investors punish, not what companies report. Identical beats now get opposite receptions depending on capex exposure
Narratives flip without warning, and once one hardens, fundamentals stop mattering in the short run. Fighting it is like fighting a ghost
A flat index can hide a genuine flight to safety. Watch rotation and breadth, not the level
When two markets price the same risk differently, tight credit spreads against obliterated equities, one of them has to give
Credit problems emerge where the growth was: subprime then, private credit and AI data center debt now
Opacity itself is the systemic risk. Small unknown losses panic everyone who might be holding the bag
Watch securitization data and bank credit quality; both lead the official statistics
Prosperity degrades underwriting. When results beat expectations year after year, standards loosen
How a sector is valued is set by consensus, what he calls the mafia. Accept the terms of debate or do not play
At perfection multiples a company cannot disappoint on any metric, actual or perceived
Cheap is not the test. An improving story beats a cheap broken one, and cheapness in software reads as a symptom
A backlog can matter more than the quarter, and a backlog is only as good as its counterparty
Never short a cult, and never assume the authorities have read the research
Know the falsifiers of your own thesis, and keep a graveyard for dead indicators as well as dead stocks
Seek the second opinion deliberately, especially against your own conclusions
Diversification means uncorrelated positions. When longs and shorts are mirror images of one trade, there is no hedge

blocks.v: If the corpus has one sentence-length summary, it is his own: investing is being practical and pragmatic. There is no one way to value stocks, no reliable oracle for turning points, and no substitute for knowing an argument well enough to measure its risk.

sections.title: How to short, according to people who do it

blocks.v: Two consecutive July 2025 episodes with boutique short researchers, Lakshmi Ganapathi of Unicus Research and Brad Safalow of PAA Research, produce the most concentrated practical material on the show. Eisman interjects his own rules throughout.

items: Never short a cult. Cultists care about things you consider irrelevant, and they buy on them. Carvana went from 83 dollars to 4 and then above 300. Ganapathi covered at the bottom and now refuses Carvana requests on principle.
Never short purely on valuation. Eisman's most-repeated rule. He says he has learned it painfully too many times to try again, and cites passing on Palantir for exactly this reason.
Never short at a 52-week high. Wait for one missed earnings. Leave money on the table rather than get run over on a breakout.
Never short a roll-up before its anniversary. Acquisition accretion masks the problem for about a year.
Never short an emotional stock. Nobody gets emotional about Stellantis. That is the point.
Beware heavily shorted names. Forced covering makes squeezes worse however good the case.
It is always the management. Investigate every board member and executive: where they worked, and why they left.
Do primary research at scale. Ganapathi called 100 to 300 car dealerships on Stellantis, and 100 to 150 solar installers to establish that advertised failure rates below 1% ran nearer 40%.
Read the balance sheet for rising receivables, rising warranty expense and rising liabilities.
Prefer secular decline to fraud. Safalow's hierarchy runs secularly challenged first, then fad, then cyclical, then fraud, because frauds persist for a decade.
Understand who owns it. His four Ps: passives, processors (quants and algos), pods, and positioning. Where passive ownership dominates, valuation barely matters and flows are everything.
Carry both kinds. High-maintenance shorts you go to war over, and set-it-and-forget-it shorts on quiet secular decline. The boring ones nobody calls about often deliver the best return on time.

blocks.v: Every single great short will have at least three to five movements against the downtrend on the way to zero. A 50 to 100% movement feels like absolute agony.

Eisman ranks short quality in three tiers. Best is a pure microeconomic short, driven entirely by company fundamentals with nothing else involved. Second is microeconomic with some macro or political overlay. Last is a short that depends on politics, because you are then betting on an administration.
He frames the psychological difference often. Being long and watching a stock rise is cheerleading. Being short is going to war, and it demands an entirely different mindset.

Delivered as formal solo lectures in two parts, Episodes 38 and 39 in December 2025, and revisited in the Big Short reflection episodes. The structure is a compact causal model he reuses to assess every new risk on the show.

rows: Too much leverage

Especially at globally systemic institutions. He blames the risk-weighted asset concept for permitting it, and pointedly not the repeal of Glass-Steagall, arguing the same loans would have been made regardless.
A large asset class blew up

Subprime mortgages. Securitisation removed funding as a constraint on growth. The industry went from 20 billion dollars of originations in 1993 to about 150 billion by 1998, died in 1999, and was resurrected by Wall Street after Greenspan cut to 1% and bond investors needed yield.
Systemic institutions owned it
The irony he stresses. By 2006 volume ran 600 billion dollars a year and Wall Street could no longer sell it all, so it kept it. The desks knew. Everyone was paid on volume, not on loan quality.
Derivatives

The only genuinely novel element. Credit default swaps tied balance sheets into a web nobody could map. It was also his instrument. He describes shorting a specific New Century 2006 BBB-minus tranche at about 3% a year, and the dawning realisation that his counterparty was repackaging his cash into a CDO.

blocks.v: The first three appear in almost every financial crisis in history, and he stresses that. Only the derivatives were new. This is why the framework travels. Applied to private credit it fails the test, because the banks are not levered and do not own the asset class in size.
The moral argument underneath

His explanation for the crisis is not stupidity, and he is emphatic about that. Asked whether incompetence causes crashes, he answered that if only that were true, we could screen for it. Instead he invokes Minsky and rational irrationality: people behave rationally inside a mania because the incentives make it rational. Chuck Prince's line about having to dance while the music plays is his exhibit. The chief executive who stops dancing earns less, underperforms, and gets fired.
Incentives trump ethics almost every time.
blocks.cite: His most-repeated maxim, stated in at least four episodes

blocks.v: He recalls asking heads of securitisation how they could make those loans, and being told it was legal. His verdict on the ratings agencies is that they earned three to four times more for subprime paper and sold their souls for the fee, and he calls the whole arrangement the biggest fraud in human history. He then bought Moody's anyway, and explains why, which illustrates fairly completely how he separates moral judgement from position-taking.

His regulatory conclusion matches what he says about capitalism generally. The question is never whether to regulate, because unregulated capitalism runs to booms and busts. The only question is how much. Too much kills the golden goose, too little returns you to the original problem, and no formula exists, only an iterative process of learning from experience.
Things that fit no single theme but recur, or are simply the most useful sentences in 923,000 words.

v: On narrative. The private credit group went from all-bullish to all-bearish with no change in fundamentals. He treats the urge to pile onto the newest narrative as a tradeable constant.
On stories. Investors love stories. Without one, nobody cares. That is his explanation for why wireless and cable languish whatever their cash flow.
On thesis clouds. When a company sits under a cloud, a bad call cannot happen. Identical guidance gets shrugged off at a beloved company and punished at a feared one.

On paradigm shifts. One of the hardest things a person goes through. The MLP investors, the 1929 bankers and the pre-crisis Wall Street executives all shared it: a paradigm that stopped being true before they stopped believing it.

On the diversification illusion. With tech near half the S&P, owning the index is not diversification. The bond sleeve does not save you either, since he cites 15% of existing corporate debt and 50% of 2026 new issuance as AI-related.
On indexing. Know what you own when you buy an index fund. A 20% single-day drop in UnitedHealth barely moved an index that finished the day up.

On captured regulators. Real, but cyclical. Pre-crisis bank regulators were as captured as possible. After the crisis they got teeth, and even a friendlier administration comes nowhere near returning to 2008 leverage.
On Long-Term Capital Management. Greenspan should have let it collapse. People would have learned better lessons.

On Ted Williams. He rereads The Science of Hitting as an investing text. The line he wrote down: swing at strikes. A good hitter on a pitch over the plate beats a great hitter reaching for a bad one in a tough spot.
On the market as economist. He endorses Verrone's line that the market is his favourite economist, along with Verrone's caution that your market call need not resemble your economic call.
On fighting the government. Delivered deadpan after an AI company was shut down over a jailbreak: it is not a great business strategy.
On hedging. If you genuinely want to hedge, the only real answer is out-of-the-money index puts. He is long-term bullish and does not advocate it.
On money market funds. Use one that holds only short-term Treasuries. You lose deposit insurance but hold government debt instead, which amounts to the same protection.
On admitting ignorance. Stated plainly during the AI depreciation debate: sometimes it is just okay to admit that you do not know.

blocks.v: Versions one and two could only count the paid episodes from the Substack archive and guess at their contents. This edition reads them. Some private-feed items are simply the public episode released a day early, so the genuinely exclusive count is 19, running from January to September 2026. They add roughly 155,000 words to the corpus, and they are not offcuts.

Two things separate the tier from the free feed. The first is length and form: this is where the uninterrupted lectures live, with no guest and no news to get through. The second is candour about himself. The portfolio episode names all 16 positions and the reasoning behind each, and the Big Short episode is the only place he audits the film that made him famous, scene by scene.
A Conspiracy of Credit, the two-part masterclass

The centrepiece, and the fullest statement of the thesis the public feed only circles. His argument runs in three steps. The United States has not had a credit-cycle recession since 2008. The post-crisis regime forced banks to delever and to stop making the riskiest loans, so that lending migrated to private credit. And privacy in that market functions as a synonym for secrecy, which means the credit built up over seventeen years is both concentrated and unobservable.

What is striking is where it lands. Given that framing, the conclusion is softer than expected: a bad credit cycle with real losses, not a systemic event. Part two drops the argument entirely and teaches the bond market from first principles, on the premise that every industry keeps a mafia whose lingo keeps outsiders out, and that underneath the jargon fixed income is common sense plus arithmetic.

v.h: Where the tier goes that the feed cannot
v.p: Boris Peaker on biotech runs 73 minutes, the longest episode in the corpus, and argues the investment map is drawn by economics rather than science: large firms can now build anything small ones can, so the real structure is a division of labour where small firms carry drugs to the finish and large firms buy them. Peter Hoffman supplies the production side of Hollywood's margin collapse, and Ben Zipursky explains why the social media suits are pleaded as product defect rather than publishing, to route around Section 230.

v.h: The sector work with no public equivalent
v.p: Brad Safalow returns for 71 minutes on the residential brokerage war, where commissions have barely moved and the real fight is over control of the MLS, plus for-profit education, which both men treat as uninvestable on the long side. Kathleen Kelly and Nancy O'Flynn make the bearish case on oil, arguing the market mistook wartime distortion for tightness. Wolfgang Munchau argues Europe's stagnation is structural, and Eisman leaves calling it pretty hopeless.

v.h: The positions he only explains here
v.p: The Glass House follow-up is the clearest example of the tier's function. He is a disclosed shareholder, rescheduling has just changed the economics, and he walks the arithmetic in public numbers: a low-cost grower capped near 200 dollars a pound in California against roughly 800 in other states. The portfolio episode does the same for the whole book.

v.h: September: the craft lectures and the hardest bear
v.p: The tier added a two-part lecture on analysing bank stocks, from leverage and loan-loss accounting to deposits, valuation and the mark-to-market mechanics that sank Silicon Valley Bank, and it is where he retires his merger thesis as a trade. Ed Zitron, the show's most complete AI bear, argues across 70 minutes that the whole ecosystem leans on two loss-making labs, and Eisman calls the dependence nerve-wracking. Lakshmi Ganapathi returns with shorts on FICO, DoorDash and AeroVironment.

blocks.v: What the paid episodes change about the public record

v: The portfolio section of this report was wrong before now. Reconstructing holdings from passing public mentions produced a list of 19 longs including names he does not own. The real book is 16, and he had already sold Alphabet, Meta and Oracle.

The consumer argument resolves behind the paywall. In the paid Ganapathi episode both sides give ground and meet: he keeps the bank credit data intact but stops treating it as a verdict on the consumer, and she concedes the stress has not surfaced in credit yet. No public episode reaches that settlement.

The Big Short corrections are on the record here. He holds that the film invents on the surface and is right underneath, names the taxi argument with his wife as invention, and reverses his own long-standing view that Steve Carell overplayed the anger, on the strength of a document rather than a memory.

Publishing moved paid-first in 2026. Three of the eighteen private-feed items are simply the public episode a day early, which is a distribution change rather than extra content, and worth knowing before anyone counts the tier by episode number.

blocks.v: One caution for anyone using this section as a buying guide. The tier is where he is least hedged, which makes it the most useful and the most dated. The oil call carries its own six to nine month clock, the cannabis case depends on a rescheduling process still running, and the portfolio is a snapshot he says would change on four named conditions. Read the dates.
Almost all the growth in lending since 2008 has been in private credit behind a veil of privacy, which means secrecy.
blocks.cite: A Conspiracy of Credit, Part 1, 13 May 2026

blocks.v: Subprime Goes to College (2010)

His second-most-famous call, and the one that most directly prefigures the podcast's moral register. He presented it at the Ira Sohn conference on 26 May 2010: a 48-page bear case on for-profit education, covering Apollo Group, ITT Educational, Corinthian Colleges and Education Management. The argument ran that these companies drew up to 90% of revenue from federal Title IV loans, posted terrible graduation and default rates, and functioned as marketing machines dressed as universities. He framed it by saying he thought he would never again find an industry as socially destructive as subprime, and had been proven wrong. He testified before the Senate HELP committee. ITT and Corinthian eventually went to zero. Brad Safalow now invokes ITT on the podcast as the template for spotting the next one.
The public record since

He has remained a fixture on CNBC, appearing on Fast Money and Squawk Box, and on Bloomberg Television, and the podcast's positions track his televised ones closely. Recent examples: pushing back on Michael Burry's market-top call as premature, warning that the market goes straight down if a hyperscaler cuts capital spending, and the August 2026 Achilles heel argument about OpenAI and Anthropic concentration. In September 2024 he publicly withdrew an earlier prediction of a Trump win and called the election a toss-up, a small but characteristic instance of retracting a call rather than defending it.
Reading his own myth

He stays consistently deflationary about the Big Short legend. He points out what the film compressed or invented, notes that his New Century short cost 40% a year to borrow, describes running the swap book and the equity book together with prices arriving an hour apart, and shows open irritation at the industry habit of predicting the end of the world. His line on the genre, that people just love to predict the end of the world, is aimed squarely at the audience that came to him for exactly that.

Each dossier ends with the questions its episode failed to settle. Collected across 92 interviews and lectures, they cluster into five arguments the show has framed carefully and cannot yet close. These are the places where the next year of episodes will either vindicate the method or embarrass it.

v.h: 1. Does the AI spend earn its return
items: The question he has refused to answer since June 2025, and dates to 2027 or 2028
Resolution test he accepts from Gary Marcus: whether tokens can be priced profitably once the subsidy ends
The dependency he named in August 2026: two private companies, Anthropic and OpenAI, continuing to buy compute
What a hyperscaler capex cut would do, which he says arrives too late to trade once it prints

Narrowed in September 2026 to one company: whether OpenAI can close a gap in which, in the June quarter, revenue rose about 1 billion dollars and costs about 3 billion, and what Anthropic's filing shows about revenue once the token subsidy ended

v.h: 2. Is private credit a cycle or a crisis
items: The dated test: software refinancings in 2027, negotiated against valuations that have already fallen
Whether buyout equity beneath the loans is itself borrowed, the Liesman insight he admits he lacked
Whether opacity alone can cause the panic without real losses ever appearing
The life insurance triangle, where he holds the thesis and concedes no credit losses have surfaced
Ganapathi's second-half-2026 call, accepted as direction and refused as date
Whether spending cracks before credit metrics, her claim and his adopted canary
Whether bank credit quality still leads, after he revised that rule in July 2026
How long a top-decile-driven economy can absorb a market correction
The 5% ten-year line, set on 18 September 2026 after 4.5% failed, with a correction called probably imminent if the yield holds above it
Whether regional banks ever merge, now a thesis he keeps for its logic and no longer invests on
Whether index concentration makes the eventual correction violent, as he predicts, or merely fast
Whether software is structurally impaired or simply early, the call he refuses to make until the data arrives

blocks.v: The fifth cluster is the one he cannot test, and he says so. Asked repeatedly to name the next black swan, he answers that the request misunderstands the term. The corpus is consistent about this: it forecasts mechanisms and refuses dates, which is exactly why the dated tests above are worth holding him to.
